title: GCSE Statistics
summary: The whole GCSE in sixteen short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Statistics specification.
subject: Statistics

title: The statistical enquiry cycle
words: Hypothesis — a statement you can test with data, such as "Year 11 students sleep less than Year 7 students"|Statistical enquiry cycle — plan, collect, process and represent, analyse and interpret, evaluate, then refine and go round again|Variable — a quantity or quality that can change from one person or item to the next|Constraint — a limit on the enquiry, such as time, cost or who you can reach|Evaluate — judge whether the data and the method really answered the question, and what to improve
points: Write the hypothesis first: every later choice, from what to collect to which chart to draw, should test it.|Hypothesis "taller people have longer arm spans": measure both on the same people, draw a scatter diagram, look for positive correlation.|A conclusion answers the hypothesis in words, using the numbers: "the Year 11 median is 40 minutes lower, so the data supports it."|An evaluation names a weakness and a fix: ten people from one class is small and may be biased, so sample fifty across the year.

title: Types of data
words: Qualitative data — described in words, such as eye colour; also called categorical data|Quantitative data — numbers that come from counting or measuring|Discrete data — can only take particular values, such as the number of brothers and sisters|Continuous data — can take any value in a range, such as height or time|Ordinal data — categories with a natural order, such as small, medium and large|Primary data — collected by you, for your own question|Secondary data — collected by somebody else, such as census results or a published table|Bivariate data — two variables measured on each item, such as the height and the mass of each person|Class boundaries — the true lower and upper limits of a group of continuous data
formulas: Class width — width = upper class boundary − lower class boundary|Class midpoint — midpoint = (lower boundary + upper boundary) / 2
points: Shoe size is discrete (there is no size 7.3), but the length of a foot is continuous.|Ages 10–14 in whole years have class boundaries 10 and 15, because somebody aged 14 years 11 months is still 14. Width = 5.|Lengths to the nearest cm grouped 20–24 have boundaries 19.5 and 24.5. Width = 5.|The midpoint of 10 ≤ t < 20 is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15.|Primary data fits your question but costs time; secondary data is quick but may be old or measured differently.

title: Populations and sampling
words: Population — everyone or everything the question is about|Census — data collected from every member of the population|Sample — the part of the population that data is collected from|Sampling frame — a list of every member of the population, which a sample is chosen from|Simple random sample — every member has the same chance of being picked, for example by numbering them and using random numbers|Systematic sample — every kth member of a list, after a random start|Stratified sample — the population is split into groups and each group is sampled in proportion to its size|Quota sample — people are picked until a set number from each group is reached; quick, but not random|Cluster sample — the population is split into clusters, some clusters are chosen at random, and everybody in them is sampled|Opportunity sample — whoever is easiest to reach; also called a convenience sample, and likely to be biased|Bias — a systematic error that makes the results unrepresentative
formulas: Stratified sample — number from a group = (group size) / (population size) × sample size|[H] Petersen capture–recapture — N = (M × n) / m, where M are marked first, n caught second, m of those marked
points: 600 students, 240 in Year 7, sample of 50: Year 7 gets 240 / 600 × 50 = 20.|Round each stratum to whole people, then check the numbers still add up to the sample size.|Systematic: 500 names, sample of 25, so k = 500 ÷ 25 = 20. Random start 7, then 7, 27, 47, …|[H] 40 fish marked; later 50 caught, 8 marked: N = (40 × 50) / 8 = 250. Assumes no births, deaths or moves in between.|A census gives complete information but takes time and money; a sample is quicker but may not represent everybody.

title: Collecting data
words: Questionnaire — a set of written questions that people answer themselves|Open question — any answer is allowed; rich, but hard to analyse|Closed question — the answer is chosen from given options; easy to analyse|Leading question — wording that pushes towards one answer, such as "Don't you agree that…?"|Pilot study — a small trial run that finds problems before the main survey|Explanatory variable — the variable that is changed or controlled; also called the independent variable|Response variable — the variable that is measured; also called the dependent variable|Extraneous variable — anything else that could affect the result, which should be kept the same|Control group — a group given no treatment, to compare against|Laboratory experiment — carried out under controlled conditions|Field experiment — carried out in a real setting, with some variables controlled|Natural experiment — the explanatory variable is not controlled by the researcher|Data cleaning — finding and fixing errors, gaps and impossible values before the analysis
points: Answer boxes must not overlap and must cover every answer: 0–1, 2–3, 4 or more, not 0–2, 2–4.|Not "How much TV do you watch?" but "How many hours of TV did you watch yesterday?" with tick boxes.|Does fertiliser help plants grow? Fertiliser is explanatory, height is response; keep water, light and soil the same.|A pilot study might show a question is misunderstood or an option is missing, so it is fixed before the real survey.|Cleaning: an age of 150 or a blank height is checked or removed before anything is calculated.

title: Tables
words: Tally — marks in groups of five, used to count while collecting|Frequency — how many times a value or a class occurs|Grouped frequency table — the data is counted in classes rather than single values|Class interval — the range of values in one class, such as 10 ≤ t < 20|Two-way table — frequencies for two variables at once, with row and column totals
points: 30 students, 18 of them girls: the table's missing entry is 30 − 18 = 12 boys.|Write classes as inequalities so they cannot overlap: 0 ≤ t < 10, 10 ≤ t < 20.|Grouping loses the exact values, so anything worked out from a grouped table is an estimate.|Check the grand total twice: it must equal the sum of the row totals and the sum of the column totals.

title: Charts for categories
words: Pictogram — symbols that each stand for a set number of items, with a key|Bar chart — bars of equal width with gaps between them; the height shows the frequency|Composite bar chart — each bar is split into parts showing the categories inside it|Comparative bar chart — bars for two or more groups drawn side by side|Pie chart — a circle split into sectors, each angle in proportion to its frequency|Population pyramid — a back-to-back bar chart of a population by age and sex|Choropleth map — a map shaded so that darker areas show higher values|Misleading diagram — a chart that gives a false impression, for example an axis that does not start at zero or an uneven scale
formulas: Pie chart angle — angle = frequency / (total frequency) × 360°|[H] Comparative pie charts — r₂ / r₁ = √(n₂ / n₁), because the area is in proportion to the total
points: 60 people, 15 chose blue: angle = 15 / 60 × 360° = 90°.|Reading back: a 72° sector of 200 people is 72 / 360 × 200 = 40 people.|[H] Totals 100 and 400: r₂ / r₁ = √(400 / 100) = 2, so a 3 cm pie becomes 6 cm.|A pie chart compares proportions; to compare actual numbers, use a bar chart.

title: Charts for numbers
topics: Stem & Leaf Diagrams, Frequency Polygons, Histograms
words: Stem-and-leaf diagram — every value shown, split into a stem and a leaf, with a key|Back-to-back stem-and-leaf — two data sets sharing one stem, for comparing|Frequency polygon — points at the midpoint of each class, joined by straight lines|Histogram — bars for continuous data, with no gaps between them|[H] Frequency density — the frequency per unit of class width; the height of a bar when the widths are unequal|[H] Bar area — in a histogram, the area of each bar is in proportion to its frequency
formulas: [H] Frequency density — frequency density = frequency / (class width)|[H] Frequency from a histogram — frequency = frequency density × class width
points: Key: stem 3, leaf 7 means 37. Leaves go in order, so stem 3 reads 1 4 4 8, never 4 1 8 4.|Class 20 ≤ x < 30 with frequency 6: plot the frequency polygon point at (25, 6).|[H] Class 10 ≤ t < 25, frequency 30: frequency density = 30 ÷ 15 = 2.|[H] A bar from 40 to 50 at height 1.6: frequency = 1.6 × 10 = 16.

title: Averages
topics: Mean, Median, Mode, Averages from a Table, Averages from Grouped Data
words: Mean — the total of the values divided by how many there are|Median — the middle value once the data is in order|Mode — the most common value|Modal class — the class with the highest frequency|Weighted mean — a mean in which some values count for more than others|[H] Geometric mean — the nth root of the product of n values; the average for growth rates
formulas: Mean — x̄ = Σx / n|Mean from a frequency table — x̄ = Σfx / Σf|Position of the median — (n + 1) / 2|Weighted mean — weighted mean = Σwx / Σw|[H] Geometric mean — geometric mean = (x₁ × x₂ × … × xₙ)^(1/n)
points: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13: mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8, median = 7, mode = 7.|x = 0, 1, 2 with f = 5, 8, 7: Σfx = 22 and Σf = 20, so the mean is 1.1.|From grouped data, use each class midpoint as x, so the mean is an estimate.|Coursework 60 with weight 1, exam 80 with weight 3: (60 + 240) ÷ 4 = 75.|[H] Growth of 10% then 21%: √(1.10 × 1.21) = √1.331 ≈ 1.154, so about 15.4% a year.

title: Measures of spread
topics: Range, Box Plots & Quartiles, Cumulative Frequency
words: Range — the largest value minus the smallest|Lower quartile — Q₁, a quarter of the way through the ordered data|Upper quartile — Q₃, three quarters of the way through the ordered data|Interquartile range — the spread of the middle half of the data|Percentile — the value below which a given percentage of the data lies; deciles split it into tenths|Cumulative frequency — a running total of the frequencies|Box plot — the minimum, Q₁, median, Q₃ and maximum drawn against a scale|Outlier — a value a long way from the rest of the data|[H] Variance — the mean of the squared distances from the mean|[H] Standard deviation — the square root of the variance; spread in the data's own units
formulas: Range — range = largest − smallest|Interquartile range — IQR = Q₃ − Q₁|Outliers — below Q₁ − 1.5 × IQR or above Q₃ + 1.5 × IQR|[H] Standard deviation — σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)^2 / n)|[H] Standard deviation, quicker form — σ = √(Σx^2 / n − x̄^2)|[H] From a frequency table — σ = √(Σfx^2 / Σf − x̄^2)
points: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12: median = 7, Q₁ = 4, Q₃ = 10, IQR = 6.|Q₁ = 20 and Q₃ = 30, so IQR = 10 and the limits are 5 and 45: a value of 52 is an outlier.|Cumulative frequency is plotted at upper class boundaries; read the median at n / 2.|[H] 2, 4, 6: mean 4, Σx^2 = 56, σ = √(56 / 3 − 16) ≈ 1.63.

title: Comparing data and skewness
words: Skewness — how lopsided a distribution is|Positive skew — the tail is to the right; usually mode < median < mean|Negative skew — the tail is to the left; usually mean < median < mode|Symmetrical — the mean, median and mode are about equal|[H] Standardised score — how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean
formulas: [H] Skewness — skew = 3(mean − median) / (standard deviation)|[H] Standardised score — z = (value − mean) / (standard deviation)
points: Compare an average AND a spread, in context: "A's median, 62, is higher than B's, 55, so A did better on average; A's IQR is smaller, so A was more consistent."|From a box plot: if Q₃ − Q₂ is bigger than Q₂ − Q₁, the data is positively skewed.|[H] Mean 50, median 47, standard deviation 6: skew = 3 × 3 ÷ 6 = 1.5, positive.|[H] Maths 72 with mean 60 and SD 8 gives z = 1.5; English 70 with mean 64 and SD 3 gives z = 2, so English is relatively better.

title: Correlation
words: Scatter diagram — bivariate data plotted as points|Positive correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to increase|Negative correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease|No correlation — no straight-line relationship between the two|Causation — a change in one variable directly causes a change in the other; correlation alone does not show it|Line of best fit — a straight line through the middle of the points, passing through the mean point (x̄, ȳ)|Interpolation — estimating inside the range of the data; fairly reliable|Extrapolation — estimating outside the range of the data; unreliable|[H] Spearman's rank correlation coefficient — how closely two rankings agree, from −1 to +1|[H] Product moment correlation coefficient — the strength of a straight-line correlation, from −1 to +1
formulas: [H] Line of best fit — y = a + bx, where b is the gradient and a the intercept|[H] Spearman's rank — rₛ = 1 − 6Σd^2 / (n(n^2 − 1))
points: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer: correlated, but hot weather causes both.|Draw the line through (x̄, ȳ) first, and use it only inside the range of the data.|[H] Marks y = 12 + 0.5x for x hours of revision: each extra hour is worth about half a mark.|[H] n = 5 and Σd^2 = 4: rₛ = 1 − (6 × 4) / (5 × 24) = 0.8, strong positive agreement.

title: Time series
words: Time series — data recorded at regular intervals over time|Trend — the general direction over a long time|Seasonal variation — a pattern that repeats every year, quarter or week|Moving average — the mean of a fixed number of consecutive values, moved along one at a time; it smooths out the seasons|Trend line — a line of best fit drawn through the moving averages|[H] Mean seasonal variation — the average gap between the actual values and the trend for one season
formulas: 4-point moving average — (sum of 4 consecutive values) / 4|Seasonal variation — seasonal variation = actual value − trend value|[H] Prediction — prediction = trend value + mean seasonal variation
points: Quarterly sales 20, 30, 40, 50, 60: the first 4-point moving average is 140 ÷ 4 = 35, the next 180 ÷ 4 = 45.|Plot each moving average at the middle of the values it uses.|Match the moving average to the cycle: 4 points for quarters, 12 for months.|[H] The trend line reads 80 next spring and spring's mean seasonal variation is −6, so predict 74.

title: Index numbers and rates
words: Index number — compares a value with the value in a base year, which is set at 100|Base year — the year all the others are compared with|[H] Chain base index — compares each year with the year before it|Weighted index — several index numbers combined, each weighted by how much it matters|RPI and CPI — official index numbers that track how prices change|Crude rate — the number of events for every 1000 people in the population|[H] Standardised rate — a rate adjusted to a standard population's age structure, so places can be compared fairly
formulas: Index number — index = value / (base year value) × 100|[H] Chain base index — index = (this year's value) / (last year's value) × 100|Weighted index — weighted index = Σ(index × weight) / Σweight|Crude rate — crude rate = (number of events) / population × 1000|[H] Standardised rate — standardised rate = Σ(rate for an age group × standard population fraction for that group)
points: £40 in the base year and £46 now: index = 46 / 40 × 100 = 115, a 15% rise.|An index of 120 is not £120; it means 20% more than in the base year.|60 births in a town of 4000: crude birth rate = 60 / 4000 × 1000 = 15 per 1000.|[H] Chain base 105 then 110: the second year rose 10%, and over both years 1.05 × 1.10 = 1.155, a 15.5% rise.|[H] A seaside town full of retired people has a high crude death rate; compare standardised rates instead.

title: Estimation and quality assurance
words: Estimate — a value for the population worked out from a sample|Sample mean — the mean of a sample, used to estimate the population mean|Sample proportion — the fraction of a sample with some property, used to estimate the population proportion|Reliability — bigger random samples give estimates that vary less|Control chart — sample results from a process plotted over time, with a target value and limits|Warning limits — a sample outside them means take another sample|Action limits — a sample outside them means stop and adjust the process
formulas: Estimating a population total — total ≈ sample proportion × population size|[H] Control limits — warning: target ± 2 standard deviations; action: target ± 3 standard deviations
points: 12 of a sample of 50 are left-handed: in a school of 1200, expect about 12 / 50 × 1200 = 288.|A machine fills 500 g bags; sample means 497 g, 502 g and 499 g stay inside the warning limits, so carry on.|One sample mean outside an action limit: stop the machine and reset it.|Two samples of the same size give different means; that is natural variation, and it shrinks as samples get bigger.

title: Probability
topics: Basic Probability, Listing Outcomes & Sample Space, Relative Frequency & Expectation, Venn Diagrams & Set Notation, Tree Diagrams, Conditional Probability
words: Outcome — one possible result of an experiment|Event — one or more outcomes, such as "an even number"|Sample space — the list of every possible outcome|Mutually exclusive — two events that cannot happen at the same time|Independent — the outcome of one event does not change the probability of the other|Relative frequency — how often an event happened, as a fraction of the trials; an estimate of the probability|Expected frequency — how many times an event should happen in a number of trials|Venn diagram — overlapping circles showing which outcomes are in which events|[H] Conditional probability — the probability of one event given that another has happened
formulas: Complement — P(not A) = 1 − P(A)|Relative frequency — relative frequency = frequency / (number of trials)|Expected frequency — expected frequency = probability × number of trials|Mutually exclusive events — P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)|Independent events — P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)|[H] Any two events — P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)|[H] Conditional probability — P(B given A) = P(A and B) / P(A)
points: Two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT, so P(one head and one tail) = 2 / 4 = 1 / 2.|Red came up 18 times in 60 spins: relative frequency 0.3, so expect about 0.3 × 200 = 60 reds in 200 spins.|3 red and 2 blue, two picks with replacement: P(both red) = 3 / 5 × 3 / 5 = 9 / 25.|[H] The same bag without replacement: P(both red) = 3 / 5 × 2 / 4 = 3 / 10.|[H] 12 study Spanish and 5 of them study French too: P(French given Spanish) = 5 / 12.

title: Probability distributions
words: Probability distribution — every value a variable can take, with its probability; the probabilities add up to 1|Binomial distribution — the number of successes in n independent trials, each with the same probability p of success|Normal distribution — a symmetrical, bell-shaped distribution of continuous data, with mean, median and mode equal|Trial — one go of the experiment, with exactly two outcomes: success or failure
formulas: Binomial — P(X = r) = nCr × p^r × (1 − p)^(n − r)|Normal: about 68% of values lie within — mean ± σ|Normal: about 95% of values lie within — mean ± 2σ|Normal: almost all, about 99.7%, lie within — mean ± 3σ
points: A fair coin thrown 3 times: P(exactly 2 heads) = 3C2 × 0.5^2 × 0.5 = 3 × 0.125 = 0.375.|Binomial needs a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, independent trials and the same p every time.|Heights normal with mean 165 cm and SD 7 cm: about 95% lie between 151 cm and 179 cm.|A value more than 3 standard deviations from the mean is very unusual, and worth checking as an outlier.
